questions.q: Dynamics is the study of motion:
options: along with the causes (forces) of motion
questions.explanation: Dynamics connects force and motion; kinematics ignores causes.

questions.q: Force is a ______ quantity which changes or tends to change the state of a body.
questions.explanation: Force has magnitude and direction.

questions.q: A batter hitting a cricket ball is an example of:
questions.explanation: There is physical contact between bat and ball.

questions.q: The force perpendicular to the contact surface that keeps objects from passing through each other is:
questions.explanation: 'Normal' means perpendicular; e.g. the table pushing up on a book.

questions.q: The force that propels a rocket or aeroplane in the direction of motion is:
questions.explanation: Engines produce thrust.

questions.q: Friction always acts:
options: opposite to the motion or attempted motion
questions.explanation: Friction resists relative motion of surfaces in contact.

questions.q: Air resistance is a type of:
questions.explanation: It is friction between air and a moving object.

questions.q: The force transmitted through a string, rope or cable is called:
questions.explanation: Tension, e.g. strands of a spider web pulling on one another.

questions.q: The force with which a stretched spring or rubber band resists change in its shape is:
questions.explanation: Elastic forces arise from forces between particles of the material.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-contact force?
questions.explanation: Magnets push or pull without touching — action at a distance.

questions.q: The force between a positively charged nucleus and a negatively charged electron is:
questions.explanation: Attraction/repulsion between charges is electrostatic force.

questions.q: The force experienced by the Moon due to the Earth is:
questions.explanation: Attraction between two masses is gravitational force.

questions.q: The strongest of all the fundamental forces is the:
questions.explanation: It holds protons tightly together in the nucleus.

questions.q: The weakest of the fundamental forces is the:
questions.explanation: Gravity is noticed only when at least one object is very massive.

questions.q: The strong nuclear force keeps protons in the nucleus by overcoming their:
questions.explanation: Like-charged protons repel; the strong force overcomes this.

questions.q: The range of the strong nuclear force is nearly equal to the:
questions.explanation: It is a very short-range force.

questions.q: The exchange particle of the electromagnetic force is the:
questions.explanation: The massless photon gives the EM force infinite range.

questions.q: Normal force, friction and tension are actually results of the:
questions.explanation: They come from interactions of charged particles at contact surfaces.

questions.q: The proposed exchange particle of gravity, not yet detected, is the:
questions.explanation: The graviton is the only exchange particle not yet detected.

questions.q: The weak nuclear force is responsible for:
questions.explanation: It changes the type of quark, turning a neutron into a proton.

questions.q: According to the book, the weak nuclear force is about how many times weaker than the strong nuclear force?
questions.explanation: The book states it is 10 000 times weaker than the strong force.

questions.q: The fundamental force with the shortest range is the:
questions.explanation: The weak force has the shortest range of all.

questions.q: The Pakistani physicist who helped unify the electromagnetic and weak forces (electroweak theory) is:
questions.explanation: Abdus Salam, with Weinberg and Glashow, developed the electroweak theory.

questions.q: After the electroweak unification, the fundamental forces are counted as:
questions.explanation: Gravitational, electroweak and strong nuclear — three fundamental forces.

questions.q: The weak force is carried by massive particles called:
questions.explanation: Their large mass limits the range of the weak force.

quizzes.topic: Free Body Diagrams and Net Force

questions.q: A diagram in which only the object being analysed is drawn with arrows showing all forces acting on it is a:
questions.explanation: A free body diagram (FBD) isolates the object.

questions.q: In a free body diagram, the length of each force arrow is:
options: proportional to the magnitude of the force
questions.explanation: Arrows are drawn to scale with their magnitudes.

questions.q: The single force having the same effect as all the forces acting on a body is called:
questions.explanation: Resultant and net force are used interchangeably.

questions.q: If the net force on an object is 0 N, the forces are:
questions.explanation: Balanced forces produce no change in motion.

questions.q: Forces of 10 N and 6 N act on a box in the same direction. The net force is:
questions.explanation: Like parallel forces are added: 10 + 6 = 16 N.

questions.q: Forces of 10 N to the right and 6 N to the left act on a box. The net force is:
questions.explanation: Unlike parallel forces are subtracted: 10 − 6 = 4 N in the direction of the larger force.

questions.q: In a tug of war, both teams pull with 500 N in opposite directions. The rope:
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite forces cancel; net force is zero.

questions.q: Three forces of 5 N, 7 N (right) and 8 N (left) act on a body. The net force is:
questions.explanation: 12 N right − 8 N left = 4 N right.

questions.q: For a book lying at rest on a table, the forces in its free body diagram are:
options: weight downward and normal force upward
questions.explanation: Weight (F_g) down and normal force (F_N) up, balancing each other.

questions.q: When forces act at an angle to each other, the resultant is found by:
questions.explanation: Vectors at an angle are added graphically by head-to-tail rule.

questions.q: An unbalanced net force on an object always produces:
questions.explanation: Unbalanced forces change speed and/or direction.

quizzes.topic: Newton's First Law, Mass and Inertia

questions.q: Newton presented his three laws of motion in 1686 in the book:
questions.explanation: Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica.

questions.q: Newton's first law states that if the net external force on an object is zero, the object:
options: maintains its state of rest or uniform motion
questions.explanation: F_net = 0 ⇒ Δv = 0, a = 0.

questions.q: The natural tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform motion is called:
questions.explanation: That is why the first law is called the law of inertia.

questions.q: Mass is a measure of the:
options: quantity of matter and inertia of a body
questions.explanation: Greater mass means greater inertia.

questions.q: Which has the greatest inertia?
questions.explanation: Inertia depends on mass; the loaded truck has the most mass.

questions.q: When a bus suddenly starts moving, standing passengers fall:
questions.explanation: The upper body tends to stay at rest due to inertia.

questions.q: When a moving bus suddenly stops, passengers fall:
questions.explanation: The body tends to keep moving due to inertia.

questions.q: When a bus turns around a curve, passengers tend to move:
options: towards the centre of the curve
to the outer side, continuing straight ahead
questions.explanation: Inertia makes them continue in a straight line.

questions.q: A card on a glass with a coin on it is flicked away quickly; the coin falls into the glass because of:
questions.explanation: The coin stays at rest horizontally, then gravity pulls it down.

questions.q: On Earth, a rolling ball eventually stops because of:
questions.explanation: External forces like friction retard its motion.

questions.q: A passenger pushing the walls inside a moving train does not change the train's velocity because the push is:
questions.explanation: Only external net forces change the velocity of a system.

questions.q: An object in free space, moving with no net force, will:
questions.explanation: No friction and negligible gravity — it keeps constant velocity.

questions.q: According to Newton's second law, acceleration is:
options: directly proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass
questions.explanation: a = F_net / m.

questions.q: The mathematical form of Newton's second law is:
questions.explanation: F_net = m a.

questions.q: One newton is the force that produces an acceleration of 1 m/s² in a mass of:
questions.explanation: 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s² = 1 kg m s⁻².

questions.q: If the net force on a body is doubled (mass constant), its acceleration:
questions.explanation: a ∝ F.

questions.q: If the mass is doubled with the same net force, the acceleration:
A 3000 N engine force acts on a bus of mass 12 000 kg. Its acceleration is:
The same 3000 N force acts on a car of mass 1200 kg. Its acceleration is:
The direction of acceleration produced by a net force is:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is in the direction of the net force.

questions.q: A force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg mass. The acceleration is:
What force is needed to give a 1500 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
Newton's first law can be deduced from the second law because if F = 0 then:
questions.explanation: F = ma = 0 ⇒ a = 0 ⇒ rest or uniform velocity.

questions.q: A boy lifts a 2 kg book upward with acceleration 3 m/s² (g = 9.8 m/s²). The total force he applies is:

quizzes.topic: Newton's Third Law and Limitations of Newton's Laws

questions.q: Newton's third law states that whenever one object exerts a force on a second object:
options: the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first
questions.explanation: F_AB = −F_BA.

questions.q: Action and reaction forces cannot cancel each other because they:
questions.explanation: Action acts on one body and reaction on the other.

questions.q: When we kick a football, the reaction force acts on:
questions.explanation: The ball pushes back on the foot with an equal force.

questions.q: When we jump, the force that pushes us into the air is:
options: the reaction force of the ground
questions.explanation: Legs push the ground; the ground pushes us up.

questions.q: We feel pain when punching a wall because of:
options: the reaction force of the wall
questions.explanation: The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on the hand.

questions.q: A rocket moves upward because:
options: exhaust gases pushed downward exert an equal upward thrust on it
questions.explanation: This is Newton's third law (action–reaction).

questions.q: Action and reaction forces are always:
options: of the same type, equal in magnitude, opposite in direction
questions.explanation: They form a pair of the same type acting on different objects.

questions.q: The force which actually moves a car forward is:
options: friction of the road on the tyres (reaction)
questions.explanation: Tyres push the road backward; the road pushes the tyres forward.

questions.q: Newton's laws are NOT applicable to:
options: objects moving at speeds close to the speed of light
questions.explanation: At such speeds relativistic mechanics is needed.

questions.q: On the atomic (very small) scale, motion is described by:
questions.explanation: Position and acceleration are not well defined there.

questions.q: Newton's laws give a good approximation for:
questions.explanation: They work very well in everyday physics and engineering.

questions.q: Weight is defined as the:
options: quantity of matter in a body
gravitational force acting on a body
questions.explanation: W = mg; it acts towards the centre of the Earth.

questions.q: The SI unit of weight is:
questions.explanation: Weight is a force, measured in newtons.

questions.q: Mass is a ______ quantity and weight is a ______ quantity.
questions.explanation: Weight has direction (downward); mass does not.

questions.q: The weight of an 8 kg school bag on Earth (g = 9.8 m/s²) is:
On the Moon (g = 1.625 m/s²), the same 8 kg bag weighs:
questions.explanation: W = 8 × 1.625 = 13 N; its mass is still 8 kg.

questions.q: When an astronaut goes from the Earth to the Moon, his:
options: weight decreases but mass stays same
both mass and weight stay same
questions.explanation: Mass does not depend on gravity; weight does.

questions.q: A spring balance measures:
questions.explanation: The spring stretches in proportion to the applied force.

questions.q: A device that measures force electronically with high accuracy and digital readout is a:
questions.explanation: A force sensor uses an electronic gauge.

questions.q: Electronic weighing scales show mass in kg because they:
options: measure weight and divide it by g (calibrated)
questions.explanation: m = W/g; scales are calibrated to show mass.

questions.q: A boy holds a 2 kg book at rest. The force he applies is (g = 9.8 m/s²):
questions.explanation: He balances its weight: 2 × 9.8 = 19.6 N.

questions.q: An object weighs 49 N on Earth (g = 9.8 m/s²). Its mass is:
Mass of a body is measured by:
questions.explanation: Balances compare or are calibrated for mass.

questions.q: The region around a massive object where its gravitational force is operative is called:
questions.explanation: E.g. the region around the Earth or the Sun.

questions.q: Gravitational field strength is the gravitational force acting per unit:
questions.explanation: g = F/m.

questions.q: The SI unit of gravitational field strength is:
questions.explanation: Newton per kilogram (N/kg).

questions.q: On the Earth's surface, the gravitational field strength is:
questions.explanation: g = 9.8 N/kg, equal in value to 9.8 m/s².

questions.q: N kg⁻¹ is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: N/kg = (kg m s⁻²)/kg = m s⁻².

questions.q: The direction of gravitational field strength on Earth is:
options: towards the centre of the Earth
questions.explanation: It is a vector pointing in the direction of gravitational force.

questions.q: As we move away from the Earth's surface, the gravitational field strength:
questions.explanation: Gravity weakens with distance from the Earth.

questions.q: A 1 kg object at the Earth's surface experiences a force of:
A body has a weight of 150 N on a planet where its mass is about 40.3 kg. The field strength there is about:
questions.explanation: g = W/m ≈ 150 ÷ 40.3 ≈ 3.7 N/kg, the value for Mars.

questions.q: Gravitational field strength and acceleration due to gravity are:
options: equal in magnitude, so the same symbol g is used
questions.explanation: g = F/m = a, so 9.8 N/kg = 9.8 m/s².

questions.q: A 60 kg astronaut on a planet with g = 24.8 N/kg weighs:
Momentum of a body is the product of its:
questions.explanation: p = m v.

questions.q: Momentum is a ______ quantity in the direction of ______.
questions.explanation: It points in the direction of velocity.

questions.q: The SI unit of momentum is:
questions.explanation: kg m/s; and N s = kg m s⁻² × s = kg m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A 45 g golf ball moves at 80 m/s. Its momentum is:
In terms of momentum, Newton's second law states that net force equals:
options: time rate of change of momentum
questions.explanation: F = Δp/Δt = (mv_f − mv_i)/Δt.

questions.q: Impulse is defined as:
options: force × time interval for which it acts
questions.explanation: J = F × Δt = Δp.

questions.q: Impulse is equal to the:
questions.explanation: F Δt = Δp.

questions.q: In a force-time graph, impulse is given by the:
questions.explanation: Area = force × time = impulse.

questions.q: A force acts on a body for 2 s and changes its momentum by 50 kg m/s. The force is:
A 1200 kg car moving at 8 m/s is stopped in 5 s. The average force required is:
questions.explanation: F = (0 − 1200 × 8) ÷ 5 = −1920 N (opposite to motion).

questions.q: Cricket gloves are padded with foam so that while catching the ball:
options: the time of impact increases and force decreases
questions.explanation: Same Δp over longer Δt means smaller force.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball moving at 15 m/s stops in 0.2 s in sand. The force by the sand on the ball is:
A system on which the net external force is zero is called:
questions.explanation: Its interactions with the environment have no effect.

questions.q: The law of conservation of momentum states that the momentum of an isolated system:
questions.explanation: If no net external force acts, total momentum cannot change.

questions.q: Before firing, the total momentum of a gun and bullet at rest is:
questions.explanation: Both are at rest, so p = 0.

questions.q: After firing, the gun moves backward. This is called:
questions.explanation: The gun gains momentum opposite to the bullet.

questions.q: The recoil velocity of a gun is small compared with the bullet's velocity because the gun:
questions.explanation: m_g v_g = −m_b v_b; bigger mass ⇒ smaller velocity.

questions.q: A 17 g bullet is fired at 350 m/s from a 3 kg rifle. The recoil velocity is about:
A 100 g bullet is fired at 20 m/s from a 5 kg gun. The recoil speed of the gun is:
A rocket accelerates in empty space because:
options: hot gases rush out with large momentum and the rocket gains equal and opposite momentum
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum (and Newton's third law).

questions.q: A man on a frictionless (oily) floor can move out by:
options: throwing his bag in the opposite direction
questions.explanation: The bag gains momentum one way; he gains equal momentum the other way.

questions.q: In the expression m_g v_g + m_b v_b = 0, the negative sign of v_g shows that:
options: the gun moves opposite to the bullet
questions.explanation: Velocities of gun and bullet are in opposite directions.

questions.q: Two skaters at rest push each other apart. Their total momentum after pushing is:
options: equal to the heavier skater's momentum
questions.explanation: Initial momentum is zero, and it is conserved.

questions.q: Inertia of a body is related to which of the following quantities?
questions.explanation: Inertia depends on mass: greater mass, greater inertia.

questions.q: A force of 5 N is applied to a body weighing 10 N. Its acceleration in m/s² is (take g ≈ 10 m/s²):
SI unit of linear momentum is:
questions.explanation: p = mv, so kg × m/s = kg m s⁻¹.

questions.q: The rate of change of momentum of a freely falling body is equal to its:
questions.explanation: Δp/Δt = net force = its weight (mg).

questions.q: Change in momentum of a body is equal to:
questions.explanation: Δp = F × Δt (impulse).

questions.q: A book of mass 5 kg is placed on the table. The magnitude of the normal (reaction) force by the table on the book is (take g ≈ 10 m/s²):
questions.explanation: The table balances its weight: mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N (net force on the book is zero).

questions.q: Thrust force is a consequence of which law of motion?
questions.explanation: Gases pushed backward push the engine forward — action and reaction.

questions.q: A force acts on a body for 2 seconds and it produces 50 kg m/s change in its momentum. The force acting on the body is:
At the fairground (rotor ride), the force that balances your weight is:
questions.explanation: Friction between your back and the wall acts upward and balances your weight.

questions.q: When a hanging carpet is beaten by a stick, dust flies off the carpet. It is mainly due to:
options: rate of change of momentum of carpet
questions.explanation: The carpet moves suddenly but the dust stays at rest due to inertia and separates.

questions.q: A bucket having some water is revolved in a vertical circle. Water does not spill out even when the bucket is upside down, due to:
options: action and reaction balance each other
questions.explanation: The water's inertia keeps it moving along its path, pressing it into the bucket.

questions.q: The force which moves the car is:
options: force of friction between road and tyre
questions.explanation: Tyres push the road back; the road's frictional reaction pushes the car forward.

questions.q: N kg⁻¹ is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: N/kg = kg m s⁻²/kg = m s⁻².

questions.q: An object of mass 1 kg placed at Earth's surface experiences a force of:
Net force on a body falling in air with uniform velocity is equal to:
options: difference of weight and air resistance, which is non-zero
questions.explanation: Uniform velocity means zero acceleration, so net force = 0.
